channel.title: Exoplanet Papers | Daily arXiv Summaries
channel.description: Daily summaries of exoplanet research papers from arXiv astro-ph.EP, written for general audiences.

item.title: Microbial Methanogenesis on Mars: A Life Detection Target for an MLE-Type Mission and Future Human Exploration
item.dc:creator: Rachel L. Harris
item.description: Why It Matters Methane is a simple gas, made of one carbon atom surrounded by four hydrogen atoms. On Mars it has become a stubborn puzzle. On Earth, living microbes produce most of our methane, although some geological processes can make it too. Spacecraft and instruments have reported what look like seasonal rises and falls, and localized plumes, of methane on Mars. Other researchers argue it has never been conclusively detected at all. If methane is really there, and if life made it, that would be one of the biggest discoveries in the history of science. What They Did This paper surveys a lively area of research rather than reporting a single new measurement. Scientists in this field ask whether microbial methanogenesis could work in the shallow Martian underground. Methanogenesis is a way for microbes to make a living by producing methane, and it is one of the simplest and most ancient forms of metabolism known. Think of it as asking whether a very hardy tenant could survive in a harsh, remote basement. The studies examine a range of extreme physical and chemical conditions found in that environment. Key Findings The emerging consensus is a cautious but encouraging "possibly." Microbes that make methane could plausibly operate under the extreme conditions of the Martian shallow subsurface. Because of this, the authors rank methanogenesis as a top-priority candidate biosignature, meaning a chemical sign that could point to life that exists on Mars today. The abstract is clear that this does not prove life is there. The origin of Martian methane, and even how reliably it has been detected, remains an open question. Looking Forward The authors argue that these results justify urgently developing better instruments that can work directly on Mars. Those instruments would need to detect methane with confidence and help show whether it comes from biology or from non-living processes. The paper frames this as a target for a Mars Life Explorer-type mission, a mission concept focused on searching for life, and for future human exploration of Mars.

item.title: Granulation in Color: The Chromatic Stellar Flicker of LTT-9779 and WASP-121
item.dc:creator: William C. Waalkes et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Stars are not perfectly steady lamps. Like a pot of simmering soup, the outer layers of Sun-like stars bubble constantly, with hot gas rising and cooler gas sinking. This churning creates a patchwork of bright and dark cells on the stellar surface, called granulation. We cannot see individual cells on distant stars, but together they make a star's brightness flicker randomly over minutes to hours. For astronomers studying planets, this flicker is a source of noise that can muddy measurements of starlight. Knowing how strong it is, and whether it looks different in different colors of light, helps us read planetary signals more cleanly. What They Did The team reused publicly available observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), taken with an instrument called NIRISS SOSS that splits starlight into a rainbow of near-infrared colors. They studied two stars: LTT-9779, a Sun-like star, and WASP-121, a somewhat hotter one. First they subtracted the signals of the orbiting planets: dips as planets pass in front, dips as they hide behind the star, and gradual brightness changes around the orbit. What remained was the star's own flicker. They then split that flicker into fast and slow rhythms, much as you might separate bass from treble in music, and fitted a standard mathematical model to it. They did this for all the light combined, and then color by color. Key Findings For LTT-9779, the flicker has an amplitude of about 54 parts per million (roughly 0.005% of the star's brightness) and a characteristic timescale of about 4.8 minutes. For WASP-121, the amplitude is about 59 parts per million and the timescale about 6.3 minutes. The power spectra also show peaks at about 3382 and 1649 microhertz for the two stars, respectively. When the light was split into individual colors, the flicker's strength decreased toward longer wavelengths. Looking Forward The authors say this opens a new observational window on short-timescale stellar variability. It also offers a way to characterize color-dependent stellar noise in the light curves used to study transiting planets.

item.title: Companions of Hot Jupiters: two decades of radial velocity monitoring with CORALIE
item.dc:creator: Léna Parc et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Hot Jupiters are giant planets that circle their stars in just a few days, far closer than Mercury orbits our Sun. They almost certainly did not form there, so astronomers want to know how they got so close. One theory says a distant companion gave the planet a gravitational shove, sending it onto a stretched-out path that was later pulled into a tight circle. If so, the hot Jupiter's neighbors should carry clues about this violent past. What They Did The team studied 147 hot Jupiter systems found by the WASP survey (Wide Angle Search for Planets). They used nearly two decades of data, from 2007 to 2025, from the CORALIE spectrograph. This instrument measures how a star wobbles toward and away from us as unseen planets tug on it, a technique called radial velocity. Because all the systems were analyzed the same way, the results can be compared fairly. The team found or refined 13 outer giant companions. They then used a statistical method to work out how common such companions are at different orbital periods, from 10 to 6,250 days. Key Findings Companions are rare close in and more common far out. Fewer than 1 in 100 systems have a giant companion with an orbit of 10–50 days, and about 2 in 100 for 50–250 days. The rate rises to about 5 in 100 for 250–1,250 days and 17 in 100 for 1,250–6,250 days. This matches how common giant planets are around ordinary Sun-like stars. Hot Jupiters with companions tend to have longer orbital periods and more stretched-out orbits. Companion orbits are less eccentric when the hot Jupiter's period is longer, and the companion's mass compared with the hot Jupiter's grows as the gap between their orbits widens. The authors say these patterns fit high-eccentricity migration, the shove-then-settle story. Looking Forward Radial velocity cannot reveal everything about a companion, such as how tilted its orbit is. Future data from the Gaia space telescope, which tracks the tiny sideways motions of stars, combined with these long records should pin down companion masses and orbital alignments, and reveal more about how hot Jupiters formed.

item.title: Robustness of C/O and mean molecular weight under disequilibrium chemistry
item.dc:creator: Bethany Burt et al.
item.description: Why It Matters When telescopes study the atmospheres of planets beyond our solar system, scientists often boil a complex light pattern down to a few headline numbers. These include the carbon-to-oxygen ratio (C/O), the oxygen-to-hydrogen ratio (O/H), and the mean molecular weight (MMW), which is the average "heaviness" of the gas particles in an atmosphere. Researchers use these numbers to infer how planets formed. But a headline number is only as trustworthy as the measurements behind it. What They Did The team studied two kinds of worlds: hot Jupiters, giant gas planets orbiting very close to their stars, and sub-Neptunes, planets between Earth and Neptune in size. They worked out mathematically how uncertainty in the measured amounts of individual molecules carries through into each headline number. They also ran VULCAN, a computer model that simulates how starlight-driven chemistry and vertical mixing of gas reshuffle molecules. They compared the results with uncertainty levels from published analyses of real observations. Key Findings Uncertainties grew much larger for the element ratios than for MMW. The fractional uncertainties in C/O and O/H were typically about as large as the ratios themselves. That is like measuring a table as "one metre, give or take one metre." In atmospheres dominated by hydrogen and helium, the fractional uncertainty in MMW was more than two orders of magnitude smaller, meaning over a hundred times smaller. Photochemistry and mixing moved individual molecules around, but they changed C/O and MMW only slightly at the depths probed by transmission spectroscopy. This technique studies starlight filtering through a planet's atmosphere. Looking Forward C/O remains a valuable clue to atmospheric chemistry and planet formation, but it must be handled with careful accounting of uncertainty. MMW may be a steadier measure. It could offer a dependable way to connect observable atmospheres to a planet's overall makeup across whole populations of planets. This is especially promising for sub-Neptunes on either side of the "radius valley," a dip in how common planets of certain sizes are.

item.title: Single-Transit Parameter Estimation with Calibrated Uncertainties
item.dc:creator: Helem Salinas et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Imagine watching a distant streetlight for months and catching a single moment when something passes in front of it. That is the problem astronomers face with "single transits": a planet crosses in front of its star only once during the observations, dimming the starlight briefly. Telescopes such as TESS (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) collect huge amounts of data, and upcoming surveys will find even more of these one-time events. The usual methods for measuring a planet's signal depend on seeing the dip repeat and stacking the repeats together, so they don't work here. Other approaches need the star's brightness "cleaned up" first, or need prior knowledge of the star. That cleaning can distort or erase the very dip being studied. What They Did The researchers built a convolutional neural network, a type of artificial intelligence that is good at recognizing patterns. They trained it on synthetic (computer-made) light curves, which are records of a star's brightness over time. From one transit, the network estimates three things: how deep the dip is, how long it lasts, and when its midpoint occurs. It also gives calibrated uncertainties, meaning error bars that honestly reflect how much to trust each answer. They compared it with a standard method called trapezoidal least-squares fitting, which models the dip as a trapezoid. Key Findings On 120 confirmed exoplanets, both methods had comparable median errors. The baseline method failed to find the transit in 10% of cases, while the network failed in only 1%. The network also had lower mean absolute errors and needed no detrending or stellar priors. It worked well on stars with strong brightness variability, where cleaning the data would damage the signal. The team also identified 169 new transit candidates in TESS Sectors 27–60 and estimated their physical parameters. The resulting catalog includes single-transit, multi-transit and multi-planet systems. Looking Forward As surveys grow, single-transit events will become more common, and astronomers will need fast, automated ways to decide which ones deserve follow-up observations. This approach offers a scalable route to doing that, with trustworthy error bars to help prioritize targets.

item.title: A 36.34-day Sub-Neptune Candidate Transiting the Nearby K Dwarf TIC 402710280
item.dc:creator: Rishit Vora
item.description: Why It Matters Planets larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune are among the most common in the galaxy, yet our own solar system has none. Learning what they are made of means finding them around bright, nearby stars, where follow-up observations are easiest. This new candidate circles TIC 402710280, an orange K dwarf (a star somewhat cooler and smaller than the Sun) about 218 light-years away. It is a candidate, not a confirmed planet. What They Did NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has only seen this star in "full-frame images," wide snapshots of the sky rather than dedicated pointings. In those snapshots the team found four small dips in starlight, called transits, recorded between 2021 and 2026. Three independent software pipelines processed the data. Two dips fell on back-to-back orbits, and the team showed that any shorter orbital period would predict dips in covered data that are not there. They then hunted for impostors. They checked where on the sky the dimming comes from, whether a faint background star 3.5 arcseconds away could be hiding a pair of eclipsing stars, and whether a secondary eclipse appears. They also ran a statistical tool called TRICERATOPS. Key Findings The candidate orbits every 36.34 days. Each transit dims the star by about 0.2% and lasts roughly 5.3 hours. That implies a planet about 3.75 times Earth's radius with an equilibrium temperature near 498 kelvin (about 225 °C). The dimming sits within 1.5 ± 1.3 arcseconds of the target. The background-star scenario requires eclipse shapes that are disfavoured for ordinary stars. No secondary eclipse was seen, and the false-positive probability is 0.003 ± 0.004. There are caveats. No high-resolution imaging exists, so very close companions are constrained only by Gaia astrometry. The transit times wander by about 21.8 minutes from a perfectly regular clock. The authors do not decide whether that comes from instruments or from gravitational tugs by another body. A separate 3.78-day signal also appears, and its source is unknown. Looking Forward The team predicts future transit times, including one in TESS Sector 114 on 19 February 2027. Those observations, plus high-resolution imaging, could test the timing wobble and strengthen the planetary interpretation.

item.title: Kinematic structure and age of a Scorpius--Centaurus subcomponent: implications for PDS 70 planetary system
item.dc:creator: Arunima Arunima, Mike Ireland, Mark Krumholz
item.description: Why It Matters PDS 70 is a young star circled by two baby planets that astronomers have photographed directly while they are still growing inside the disk of gas and dust that made them. That makes it a benchmark for how giant planets form. But a planet's brightness only reveals its story if we know its age, much as a candle's remaining length means little unless you know when it was lit. The star's commonly used age of 5.4 million years (give or take 1 million) is much younger than the ages found for the larger stellar group it belongs to, Upper Centaurus–Lupus. What They Did Instead of judging the star's age by its brightness and color, the team traced how stars move. Stars born together drift apart over time, so running their motions backward shows when they were last bunched together. The team used the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) on the Australian National University 2.3-metre telescope to measure how fast 405 candidate members of a Scorpius–Centaurus subgroup, called the T subcomponent, move toward or away from us. These measurements were 5.5 times more precise than those from the Gaia space telescope. They combined them with Gaia's sky positions and motions in a modelling framework called Chronostar. Key Findings The T subcomponent stars have a kinematic age of roughly 10–15 million years, and PDS 70 itself comes out at about 12–16 million years. That rules out ages as young as the published 5.4 million. At this older age, the brightness of planet PDS 70 b, and to a lesser degree planet c, does not match the "warm-start" cooling models, which assume a planet begins hot and fades, given current estimates of its mass. The most natural explanation is that planet b formed about 10.5 million years after its star, and no less than about 7.7 million years after it. Looking Forward If this holds, giant planets may be able to form much later in a disk's life than many theories assume. Better mass measurements and further tests of the age will show whether the planets really are late arrivals.
